lead: A cellular operator owns a fixed slice of radio spectrum, too small to give every subscriber a separate channel. The fix is frequency reuse: the same channel is used again in a cell far enough away that the two signals do not spoil each other. Cells are drawn as hexagons, grouped into clusters, and the pattern repeats across the city. The arithmetic below gives cluster size, reuse distance and signal-to-interference ratio, then the allocation choices. Every GSM or LTE tower you use runs on this idea.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.3 for what a cell and a carrier are; here a cell is one base station's radio coverage area.

sections.h3: Cells, clusters and the hexagonal layout

blocks.text: Radio spectrum is scarce. An operator splits its area into cells, each served by one base station. The cell radius R is the distance from the centre to a hexagon corner. The operator divides its channels into groups. If every cell had its own group, the spectrum would run out. Instead a group is reused far away. The set of cells that uses every group once is a cluster, of size N cells. The cluster pattern repeats. Touching cells use different groups; cells that reuse a group are co-channel cells. The figure shows a seven-cell cluster: A is the centre, B to G its six neighbours.
A hexagon is chosen because it tiles the plane with six equal neighbours, so the worst-case distance to a neighbour is easy to write.

sections.h3: Cluster size, reuse distance and SIR

blocks.text: Choose non-negative shift integers i and j. Move i cells along one hexagon axis and j cells along the next; the landing cell may reuse the same channels.

blocks.where: N is the cluster size in cells; i and j are non-negative shift integers.
D is the reuse distance in km; R is the cell radius in km; N is the cluster size.
Q is the co-channel reuse ratio, a pure number.

blocks.text: D is the centre-to-centre reuse distance. Six co-channel cells form the first ring. With path-loss exponent k, received power falls as distance to the power k.

blocks.where: SIR is the signal-to-interference power ratio; k is the path-loss exponent, about 4 in a city and 2 in free space; 6 is the number of first-ring co-channel interferers.

blocks.text: For k = 4, SIR = (√(3N))⁴ ÷ 6 = 9N² ÷ 6 = 1.5N². A larger N raises D and lowers interference but leaves fewer channels per cell.

sections.h3: Channel allocation: fixed, dynamic, hybrid, borrowing

blocks.text: Fixed allocation gives each cell a permanent set of channels: simple, no central control, but a busy cell blocks calls while a quiet neighbour sits idle. Dynamic allocation pools all channels and assigns them on demand: it handles hot spots better but needs fast coordination to keep co-channel separation. Hybrid allocation fixes some channels per cell and keeps a pool for demand. Channel borrowing lets a busy cell use a neighbour's idle channel, provided the borrowed channel is not already used within distance D. Erlang-B gives the blocking probability for a fixed number of channels and a given offered load; one line is enough here. When a user crosses a cell boundary the call moves to the new cell; see Chapter 1.5.

figure.caption: Cell A and its six neighbours B to G make the seven-cell cluster. Two steps along a row and one step turned 60° reach the next cell that reuses group A, D = √21 R = 4.58 km away, which gives SIR 73.5 (18.66 dB) and 350 ÷ 7 = 50 channels per cell.

examples.question: A network uses a cluster with shift integers i = 2 and j = 1. Cell radius R = 1 km. Path-loss exponent k = 4. The operator owns 350 channels. Find N, D, Q, SIR in dB, and channels per cell.
examples.answer: N = 7, D = 4.58 km, Q = 4.58, SIR = 73.5 (18.66 dB), and each cell gets 50 channels.
examples.check:
import math
i, j = 2, 1
R = 1.0
k = 4
total_channels = 350
N = i*i + i*j + j*j
D = R * math.sqrt(3*N)
Q = D / R
SIR = Q**k / 6
SIR_dB = 10 * math.log10(SIR)
per_cell = total_channels / N
print(N)
print(round(D, 2))
print(round(Q, 2))
print(round(SIR, 1))
print(round(SIR_dB, 2))
print(int(per_cell))

traps: Using D = R√N instead of D = R√(3N).
Forgetting the six co-channel interferers, so SIR = Q^k instead of SIR = Q^k ÷ 6.
Writing 73.5 dB; 73.5 is a power ratio, while 18.66 dB is its dB value.
Reusing a channel in a touching cell; reuse needs the full distance D.
Swapping i and j changes nothing because N is symmetric; do not invent two different N values for (2,1) and (1,2).

quiz.a: Using the same channel group in cells separated by at least the reuse distance D.

quiz.q: Why are cells drawn as hexagons?
quiz.a: A hexagon tiles the plane with six equal neighbours, giving a simple worst-case model of coverage.

quiz.q: For i = 1, j = 1 and R = 2 km, find N, D and Q.
With k = 4 in the previous question, find SIR.
Why does a larger N improve SIR but reduce capacity?
quiz.a: Larger N increases D and Q, so interference falls. But the operator's channels split into N groups, so each cell gets fewer channels.

quiz.q: Compare fixed and dynamic channel allocation.
quiz.a: Fixed gives each cell permanent channels: simple, no central coordination, but blocks calls under uneven load. Dynamic pools all channels and assigns on demand: it serves hot spots better, but needs fast coordination and signalling to keep co-channel separation, so it costs more to run.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real networks use fractional frequency reuse and OFDMA resource blocks, so the strict hexagonal cluster is a planning model, not a physical rule. Small cells and self-organizing networks adjust reuse automatically. Search those three terms.
